analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 14% and bans fees, campus marketing, and sudden term changes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2009, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Eric Massa's bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to cap credit card interest rates at 14% APR, stop credit card companies from charging fees when a customer moves a balance from another card, and bar them from advertising on college campuses. It also would have locked in a credit card's terms so long as the cardholder kept paying on time, and required at least 30 days between the date a statement is mailed and the payment due date. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly half of American households that carry a credit card balance month to month. A 14% cap would directly lower the interest they pay; the ban on changing terms would protect customers who pay on time from sudden rate hikes; the longer due-date window would reduce late fees caused by short billing cycles; and the campus advertising ban would shield students from credit card marketing.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card accounts at 14%, directly lowering what carrying a balance costs.
Bans fees or penalties when a consumer uses one card's credit to pay down another card's balance.
Bars credit card issuers from advertising on college campuses by handing out applications or solicitations.
Prohibits an issuer from changing the terms of a card contract while the consumer is in full compliance with its existing terms.
Requires the payment due date to be at least 30 days after the statement was mailed, reducing late fees from short billing cycles.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, who would earn less from interest above 14%, from balance-transfer fees, and from penalty fees tied to short due dates. Higher-risk borrowers might also face reduced access to credit if issuers decline to lend at a capped rate.

drawbacks.text: A hard 14% cap could make lenders stop offering cards to higher-risk borrowers, reducing access to credit for people with lower incomes or poor credit histories — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh.
The cap applies to all open-end consumer credit accounts, not just cards, so the bill's restriction is broader than its title suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who carry credit card debt, the interest cap and the ban on changing terms for paying customers would be substantial, concrete benefits. The main tradeoff is credit access: a binding rate cap can push lenders away from risky borrowers. The bill never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be debated or tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee after referral and died there when the 111th Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Representative Eric Massa introduced the American Credit Card Reform Act on April 21, 2009.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
No further action was taken; it had zero cosponsors and died in committee at the end of the 111th Congress in January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers benefit, because none of the bill's restrictions — the 14% rate cap, the fee ban, the term-change ban — ever became law through this bill. Consumers who carry balances continue paying whatever rates issuers charge.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers, who faced no new limits

for.name: Eric Massa
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 21, 2009 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no party positions were recorded; the bill attracted no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would cut issuer revenue from interest above 14%, balance-transfer fees, and penalty fees tied to short due dates, and would end a marketing channel on college campuses. Cardholders carrying balances would pay less.

The campus advertising ban would end card-marketing activity on college grounds. Some institutions earn revenue from affinity card deals with issuers, so the bill would end that income stream while removing marketing aimed at students.
